The Quiet Discipline of Maintenance

By A. Fixture · Published March 3, 2024 · 6 min read

Every civilization eventually learns the same lesson twice: building something is glamorous, and keeping it working is not. Ribbon-cuttings get press releases; the crew that replaces a worn gasket at 2 a.m. gets nothing but the quiet satisfaction of the lights staying on.

Dr. Elena Marsh, an infrastructure historian, has spent two decades studying this asymmetry. “We celebrate the opening of a bridge,” she says, “but almost no one celebrates the 10,000th inspection that keeps it standing.” Her research spans the U.S., the U.K., and much of continental Europe, and the pattern repeats everywhere she looks.

Why maintenance is invisible

Part of the problem is structural. Maintenance work is defined by the absence of an event — nothing broke, nothing failed, nothing made the news. A well-maintained system is, by design, boring. Fig. 1 below illustrates the failure curve that maintenance teams are constantly trying to flatten.

There is also a budgeting problem. Capital budgets fund new construction with fanfare; operating budgets fund the unglamorous work of keeping that construction alive, and they are the first line item cut when money is tight. No. 1 on most auditors' lists of deferred-cost traps is exactly this line item.

[ Advertisement: in-article rectangle ]

What good maintenance cultures share

Across the organizations Marsh studied, three habits recurred, in roughly this order of importance:

  1. Maintenance staff have direct authority to halt operations when something looks wrong, without needing sign-off from three layers of management.
  2. Inspection logs are treated as first-class data, reviewed on a fixed cadence rather than only after an incident.
  3. Budgets separate “keep it running” money from “build something new” money, so the former can't quietly be raided for the latter.

“The organizations that do this well don't think of maintenance as a cost center. They think of it as the thing that makes every other budget line mean anything at all.” — Dr. Elena Marsh

A small, telling example

Marsh's favorite illustration is not a bridge or a power plant but a municipal water utility that tracks something as small as valve-turning frequency. Valves that are never exercised tend to seize; seized valves turn a routine shutoff into an emergency excavation. The fix costs approx. $40 per valve per year. The failure it prevents costs, on average, $18,000.

Table 1 — Cost of routine valve exercise vs. emergency replacement (illustrative)
Scenario Frequency Cost per event
Routine valve exercise Annual $40
Emergency excavation & replacement Rare, but rising $18,000

The code that maintains itself

The same asymmetry shows up in software. A small script that checks link health nightly is easy to write and easy to ignore; the following minimal example is the kind of thing that, left running for years, quietly prevents an entire class of “404 Friday” incidents. 

async function checkLinks(urls) {
  const results = await Promise.all(
    urls.map(async (url) => {
      try {
        const res = await fetch(url, { method: 'HEAD' });
        return { url, ok: res.ok, status: res.status };
      } catch (err) {
        return { url, ok: false, status: null };
      }
    })
  );
  return results.filter((r) => !r.ok);
}

Conclusion

None of this requires new technology. Fig. 2 (not shown) would simply repeat Fig. 1 with the labels swapped, which is itself the point: the shape of the problem does not change, only our willingness to fund the unglamorous middle of the curve. Vs. a ribbon-cutting, a maintenance budget line will never make the evening news. It will, however, decide whether there is a bridge left to cut a ribbon on in thirty years.
